Malka’s Story A Different Eye for the Stones Three-million-dollar deals were written on a tiny piece of silver foil torn from a cigarette pack and sealed with a handshake. That was all it took. The business was built on trust — and I built my life on it. Malka Roizen, President For nearly fifty years, Malka Roizen has built a reputation on something that cannot be weighed or graded: trust. One of the few women to own and operate an independent diamond business, Malka brings a different eye to the stones — one shaped by decades of experience, a perspective her customers have come to value as much as her legendary precision. Her clients return not simply because of the quality of her diamonds, but because they know that when Malka says a stone is a certain size, color, or quality, it is. Every time. But her story begins long before Baguette Mondial, inside Israel’s legendary diamond exchange — in a trading hall that didn’t want her there at all. Ramat Gan · 1979 The Trading Floor Malka was twenty-one years old when a family friend invited her to work with him at the diamond bourse in Ramat Gan. He became her employer and mentor, introducing her to the business and teaching her everything he knew. She studied by night and worked the floor by day, stepping each morning into a world of fortunes and back out each evening into ordinary life. It was a man’s world, and many of the religious traders objected to a woman joining them in the hall. On my first day, I was carrying a tray of coffee into the building. A man saw me and just slammed the door in my face. The coffee spilled everywhere. I was clearly not welcome. But Malka never tried to force acceptance. She simply worked. Within weeks, attitudes began to change — they went from ignoring her completely to giving her advice, even throwing her a bone occasionally. One day, while walking past a negotiation, two traders asked Malka to hold a rare fancy red diamond while they completed the paperwork. Her mentor saw what was happening and told the traders, “If she’s holding the stone, she deserves a commission.” They agreed — and Malka received a commission on the deal. The woman who had once been ignored on the trading floor was now being recognized as part of the business. Her mentor also taught her that the diamond business depended on absolute honesty. Reputation was everything. She witnessed deals worth millions of dollars recorded on small pieces of silver foil torn from cigarette packs, then finalized with a hand
